claims.text: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi typically has a coercive field below 100 Oe.
Related single-phase fcc high-entropy-alloy derivatives have coercive fields no greater than approximately 100 Oe under comparable measurement conditions.
Introducing a controlled minor L1₀-type second phase into an fcc FeCoNi matrix will substantially increase coercivity.
L1₀-type precipitates possess high magnetocrystalline anisotropy.
A thermal–mechanical treatment can induce controlled precipitation of a minor L1₀ phase within a predominantly fcc matrix.
Annealing within a narrow temperature window can produce a few-percent volume fraction of the second phase while preserving matrix integrity.
The proposed structural mediator is a population of nanoscale L1₀ precipitates structurally distinct from the fcc matrix.
The L1₀ precipitates act as pinning centers for magnetic domain walls.
Pinning by the L1₀ precipitates increases the energy barrier for domain-wall motion.
The increased barrier to domain-wall motion produces a higher coercive field than in the homogeneous single-phase alloy.
The modified alloy is predicted to have a coercive field above 100 Oe.
The modified alloy is predicted to retain saturation magnetization comparable to that of the single-phase baseline.
Minor precipitates can be thermodynamically stabilized in applicable multicomponent fcc alloys without drastically changing overall composition.
Minor-precipitate stabilization can be achieved without compromising high saturation magnetization.
The predicted effect applies at room temperature under quasi-static magnetic-field sweeps.
The precipitate volume fraction and spatial distribution determine the optimal coercivity increase and the tradeoff with saturation magnetization.
